stances.claim: The Palaña death the day after Joel Escorial's surrender -- and the divergent autopsy findings -- is 'twist of twists' that warrants Remulla's 'disbelieving coincidences' and 'suspecting foul play' posture; the second autopsy by Dr. Raquel Fortun ('first Filipino woman forensic pathologist') concluded asphyxia by plastic bag despite no significant external or internal injury, while the NBI autopsy implied natural causes.
stances.rhetorical_move: twist-of-twists scenario framing with named-expert findings

stances.claim: Murder conviction requires 'credible testimony of credible witnesses' -- which is why the NBI and police have prospective NBP-inmate witnesses, and likely why Escorial would be included as accused only to be 'discharged from the case and granted immunity as a state witness' (DOJ proposes; trial court has discretion).

The two autopsies' divergent findings create a Tuyor-vs-Lagao tension. Under People v. Tuyor (Oct. 12, 2020), a medico-legal report by a government doctor is admissible without the physician testifying -- falling under the 'entry in official records exception' to hearsay with a 'prima facie presumption of regularity.' The NBI autopsy thus enjoys admissibility-by-default. Fortun's contradictory finding must overcome that presumption.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal-tension setup (Tuyor authority for NBI report)

stances.claim: The unstated fact in the news reports is what the death certificate says. Under Lagao v. People (Sept. 15, 2021), variance between the death certificate and the autopsy report left the evidence 'in equipoise' and warranted acquittal -- making the death certificate's stated cause of death a critical missing data point in the Palaña case.

A death certificate is a 'public document' -- 'the best evidence of its content without need of any testimony,' admissible without proof of execution/genuineness, with entries 'presumed correct unless the party who contests its accuracy can produce positive, contrary evidence.' This evidentiary status makes the unreported death certificate potentially dispositive.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban surveys the Percival 'Percy Lapid' Mabasa murder case as Justice Secretary Boying Remulla prepares to file (on November 7) separate murder charges against a 'very high person' mastermind and several others in the brutal killing of the radio broadcaster and of NBP inmate Cristito 'Jun Villamor' Palaña -- with the Lapid family lawyers Berteni Causing and Danilo Pelagio already pointing to suspended Bureau of Corrections director general Gerald Bantag as the alleged mastermind of a 'multi-twisted plot reminiscent of Perry Mason mysteries (if the oldies like me will remember).' Days after Lapid was gunned down, Joel Escorial surrendered as the lone motorcycle gunman, fearing elimination by the mastermind he had never personally met; he fingered two 'middlemen' -- Palaña and Christopher Bacoto, both NBP inmates -- who contracted him for P550,000. 'Twist of twists,' a day after Escorial surrendered, Palaña died en route to the NBP Hospital; Bacoto is allegedly safely secured under BJMP custody. 'Disbelieving coincidences' and 'suspecting foul play,' Remulla ordered an NBI autopsy of the already-embalmed Palaña; unnamed NBI medico-legal experts found 'no apparent external injuries,' implying natural causes. Not satisfied, Remulla and the Lapid family asked Dr. Raquel Fortun -- 'the first Filipino woman forensic pathologist in the Philippines and head of the Department of Pathology of the University of the Philippines Manila' -- to conduct a second autopsy six days later. Fortun confirmed no 'significant injury' internal or external, but concluded the death was caused by 'asphyxia or suffocation likely by a plastic bag placed over the victim's head,' and noted 'complications in the lungs (pulmonary congestion, edema, and hemorrhages) and schistosomiasis of the liver, a parasitic disease.' For murder conviction, 'credible testimony of credible witnesses is vital' -- explaining why prospective NBP-inmate witnesses are being readied and why Escorial may be 'included as an accused; later to be discharged from the case and granted immunity as a state witness' (DOJ propose, trial court discretion). The two-autopsy divergence creates a doctrinal tension: under People v. Tuyor (October 12, 2020), the NBI medico-legal report -- by a government doctor -- is admissible without the physician's testimony under the 'entry in official records exception' to hearsay with a 'prima facie presumption of regularity.' Fortun's contradictory finding must overcome that presumption. Critically, 'the news reports did not give any info on what the death certificate said.' Under Lagao v. People (September 15, 2021), the SC acquitted the accused because of variance between the death certificate and the autopsy report -- the variance 'left the evidence in equipoise that warranted the petitioner's acquittal.' A death certificate is a public document, 'the best evidence of its content without need of any testimony,' admissible without proof of execution/genuineness, with entries 'presumed correct unless the party who contests its accuracy can produce positive, contrary evidence.'
